analytic.title: A Method for Modeling and Verification of Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems are used in many critical applications. Verification of these real-time systems is essential. Presented here is a method for modeling real-time systems and computing the model's timing characteristics automatically. From a data-driven model of the system an equivalent finite state machine representation of the system is produced by this package. To provide efficient traversal of this large state space an Ordered Binary Decision Diagram (OBDD) is used to represent the state machine using symbolic methods. Algorithms have been developed to find the largest and smallest distance (times) between any two state sets. From these algorithms schedulability of the real-time system can be determined.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Some of the most important applications of computers are embedded real-time systems. These systems are used in such areas as avionics, medical equipment, plant control, etc. Most software systems attempt to provide correct results in an efficient manner. Real-time software systems not only must be numerically correct, but also have additional specifications for the time in which the results must be delivered. Correct results are useless if, by the time they are delivered, they are too late to provide the feedback necessary to prevent system damage or failure. Human lives or valuable equipment may be at risk in the event of a failure. In systems such as data acquisition systems for jet engine testing failure to meet the deadlines could mean loss of very expensive test data. Real-time systems have well-defined, rigid timing constraints; they must process events within a given time frame. A real-time system is considered to function correctly only if it returns the correct results within the associated time constraints. Processing must be done within the defined constraints or the system will fail.

It is clear that a method to verify these hard real-time systems is necessary. The problem is that as the complexity of the system increases the number of possible execution sequences grows exponentially in size and can become too large to test. Presented here is a method to efficiently explore these very large state spaces that are encountered.

Simulation techniques are often used to verify real-time systems. These simulations do not always expose dog problem areas because all possible system states may not be explored. Theorem provers and proof checkers are also used to verify systems although these methods are very time consuming and labor intensive. These methods can become very complex for large systems. In this work a model-based approach is selected for verification of real-time systems.

Using a model-based approach allows the system to be designed and analyzed before it is actually constructed. This can allow the designer to explore "what if' scenarios and analyze different designs before actual implementation. The model of the system is translated into a Finite State Machine (FSM) representation. Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams (OBDDs) are used to symbolically represent the FSM model. The BBDDs provide an efficient way of traversing the large state space that often results. Algorithms are developed to verify that the system aZwuys meets its timing constraints to provide correct operation.

div.head: Background
div.p: Model-Based Programming Model-based programming can facilitate management of complex software systems and enable easy system generation and modification. The MultiGraph Architecture (MGA) is a software tool set used for the generation and analysis of software and systems. The basic concepts behind the design of MGA involve the use of domain-specific system modeling. By modeling a system in terms familiar to the user, some of the complexity of the system can be hidden from the user [ABB93].

With MGA, applications are generated from models that specify the system. The software produced will actually follow model of the system it is generated from mlike other design methods in which too much freedom is given between the design and implementation stages. Model-based analysis can be performed while the system is still in the design stages to gain knowledge of the system's timing characteristics [ABB93].

div.head: Modeling Environment
div.p: In the MultiGraph Architecture applications are generated from models. Entering models of a complex system into the analysis tool via text files can be tedious and hard to visualize. To facilitate the entry, the XVPE Model Editor can be used to input the models into the system. The editor provides a graphical method used to capture many types of specifications of systems in the MGA environment. In this system the editor gives a graphical method to specify our Signal Flow type model.

The models built from the editor are stored in an object-oriented database. Interpreters are built for specific applications to generate a system implementation from the models. Analysis tools such as the one discussed here can also extract system information from the models.

div.head: Systems Considered
div.p: Real-time systems that are candidates for verification by this tool are assumed to be nonpreemptive and have one periodic event such as a process that acquires a new data sample. All other processes scheduled to run during this period between which the data samples are taken must fiiish before the next sample period begins. The system is schedulable if and only if all processes are guaranteed to fiiish execution before the next sample period begins.

The processes in the system are assumed to be data driven. This creates a data dependency between processes. These dependencies are modeled by a dataflow diagram. A process is scheduled only if data is available at its inputs. Processes are chosen for execution from this schedule by their assigned priority. The systems considered are those with N number of processes each with a statically assigned priority and execution time. Only single processor systems are considered.

div.head: OBDD Representation
div.p: Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams (OBDDs) provide an efficient way to manipulate Boolean functions. They represent the function in the form of a directed acyclic graph [REB92]. The vertices of the graph are organized in levels by index. The internal vertices of a graph on the same level correspond to a particular variable of the Boolean function. All paths of the graph lead to one of the two terminal vertices labeled by the values 0 and 1. Figure 1 illustrates the OBDD for the Boolean formula (a ~b ) v c.

The ordering of the variables (the ordering of the levels within the graph) can have a dramatic effect on the size of the OBDD. A bad variable ordering can greatly increase the time required to perform operations on that OBDD and, sometimes more importantly, may be too large to fit in the computer's physical memory. For some choices of variable ordering the representation of a function can grow exponentially as the number of variables grow, while for other choices of ordering the size may only be of linear growth. By using common sense in choosing the variable ordering these problems can usually be avoided.

In this application OBDDs are used to represent a fiiite state machine. The FSM's next-state equation is represented by a single OBDD. A function is built which given a present state set returns the corresponding next state set using the next-state equation OBDD. The present state set is passed to the function as an OBDD. Its corresponding next state set is returned from the function as an OBDD in terms of the same variables. This approach gives a fast way of traversing the state space of the system. It provides a way of searching the state space without looking at each indwidual state.

div.head: Model Representation
div.p: The real-time system is modeled as a collection of processes connected in a data driven fashion.

One process is marked as the periodic process in the system with the period it is executes at. Each process has its own attributes such as execution time, priority, data inputs, data outputs, etc. In this type of system the execution of a process occurs when data is available on its inputs.

Each process may be marked as an IF-ANY or IF-ALL type of process. If the processes are to be executed when data appears on any one of its input ports then the process should be marked with the IF-ANY input discipline. If the process should execute only after data appears on all its input ports then it should be selected IF-ALL. The execution time and priority of each process must also be specified.

Two types of process output ports are available: Unconditional and Conditional. The Unconditional output specifies that the process always outputs data here every time it runs. The Conditional output port may or may not output data every time the process runs based on the data or other parameters not specified in the model. For example, a process may or may not output an alarm condition based on the magnitude of its input data. Both cases (data is output or data is not output) must be taken into consideration when building the state machine model.

div.head: Building the State Machine Representation
div.p: The dataflow representation of the model is transformed into a finite state machine representation of the system. An equivalent finite state machine representation of the system is derived from the dataflow description of the system by simulating the execution of the system. The node that is marked as being the periodic process is executed (in the simulation). The data that this process produces triggers other processes to be put into the process queue. The process with the highest priority that meets its execution constraints (IF-ALL / IF-ANY input requirements) is removed from the queue and executed. This continues until the process queue is empty and no other processes are to be run.

Processes are allowed to have the same priority. In this case the execution is simulated such that a case occurs where process A runs first then process B and another case where process B runs first then A (in terms of the state diagram the possible execution is split at this point into two branches).

If a process has a conditional output then the execution must simulate both cases: one case where the output produces data that triggers the next process to execute and the case that no output is produced. This will also cause a branching of the state diagram that can be interpreted as a nondeterministic situation.

It is clear that for systems that have processes that may or may not start other processes based on their input data and/or situations where a non-deterministic execution is modeled a very large number of possible execution sequences can be produced. Using a symbolic OBDD representation of the state machine provides the means to efficiently search this state space. The size of the OBDD representation is kept to a manageable size as the state machine grows exponentially larger.

div.head: Analysis Algorithms
div.p: Two algorithms were used for finding the longest and shortest time between state sets. The state machine's next-state equation representing the state space is passed to these functions in the form of an OBDD [CAM95]. Two state sets, an initial state set and an ending state set, are passed to the function each in the form of an OBDD. These functions return an integer specifying the longest or shortest time between these two state sets. If the system is found to have a case where it may m i s s a deadline then the sequence of events that may lead up to this event can be provided to the user.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: It is necessary to verify real-time systems in critical applications. For many systems this is a difficult task since state space of the system grows exponentially as the complexity increases. A way of examining this state space efficiently is needed. A model-based analysis method using OBDDs is well suited to this task. From the system model a finite state machine representation is automatically derived. Algorithms that can determine schedulability based on the FSM have been developed. The ability of the algorithms to analyze a large state space efficiently is made possible by using OBDDs. The OBDDs provide a representation of the fmite state machine that can be explored symbolically on a state set basis. This method provides the real-time system designer with the timing characteristics of the high-level system model. This allows the designer to evaluate system choices at design time where the decisions are most crucial.

Future directions include extending this method to verify real-time parallel processing systems where the data flow between multiple processors must be modeled. The method could also be extended to systems with multiple cyclic processes on a single processor.

figure.figDesc: The Lower bound algorithm steps through the state diagram using the next state equation. It starts with an initial state set and internally keeps a current state set. At each step it looks for an intersection of the current state set and the ending state set. A non-null intersection set means we have reached an ending state. The time that has elapsed since the beginning state is returned. Upper bound algorithm works in a similar fashion. It steps through the state diagram beginning with an initial state set and maintains a current state set at each step. This algorithm traverses the state space noting when an intersection of the current state set and the ending state set occurs. The maximum time from the initial state set until the ending state set is returned as the longest path between the two given state sets. The value of these algorithms is that individual states do not have to be examined because these functions operate on state sets that are represented symbolically.
